newsitem.title: USA: Socks trounces Leader; Halloween goes political.
newsitem.headline: Socks trounces Leader; Halloween goes political.

text.p: Socks the White House cat trounced Bob Dole's miniature Schnauzer Leader in a highly unscientific pre-election poll, with at least one diehard Democratic canine crossing species lines to back the First Cat.

In what passed for election-year drollery in a season notably lacking it, Socks Clinton, an Arkansas Democrat, beat Leader Dole, a Kansas Republican, in the race for First Pet at a fund-raiser this week to benefit the Washington Animal Rescue League.

The fix may have been in from the start, however: the honorary chairpet of the event was Bucky Shalala, a dog belonging to Donna Shalala, the secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS), a Clinton appointee.

"It was a romp," HHS spokesman Victor Zonana crowed after the Tuesday vote, which featured campaign buttons, ballots and hundreds of celebrating partisans. "Bucky, though a canine, was crossing species lines to support the First Feline."
In one respect, Leader has the edge over Socks. While Socks makes a few guest appearances on the Internet, Leader has his own website at http://www.firstdog.com/.

With a bone-shaped title, "Leader Dole, First Dog 96," the site features places to order Leader buttons and T-shirts, to learn about the 1995 hero dog Cinders, take a tour of Washington with the Dole canine and meet a few of Leader's most intimate animal Internet pals.
And of course, there is a spot for browsers to "cast your vote for Leader Dole."
The Halloween spirit emerges in stranger ways in Washington than elsewhere around the United States. On one surburban lawn, a pumpkin was carved with the possibly scary legend "Dole-Kemp".
Elsewhere in the area a yard was strewn with mock tombstones, including one with a Dole-Kemp sticker on it.

For the most part, though, the week belonged to presidential politics. At the Old Ebbitt Grill, a venerable watering hole a stone's throw from the White House, diners and drinkers cast their votes in a straw poll for President Bill Clinton, Dole or Reform Party candidate Ross Perot.
Before lunch on Thursday, Clinton was leading with 9,751 votes, Dole had 8,352 and Perot had 403. Unlike a genuine election, patrons can cast more than one ballot.

For those left numb by the constant barrage of presidential rhetoric in the election endgame, Alaska offers a respite of wild and wooly campaigning: a punch in the face, a mysterious mailing alleging adultery and a brief stop in jail.

Kenai Peninsula Borough assemblyman Mike Wiley was jailed briefly on assault and trespassing charges after striking Louie March, a legislative candidate blamed for the mailing, which described a series of fictitious and complicated sexual entanglements in Seward, Alaska, involving Wiley, incumbent state Representative Gary Davis and other officials.

Its author was unclear but all five people named as adulterers fingered March, a 40-year-old cannery worker and political gadfly who is running for the state legislature on the ticket of the fringe Alaskan Independence Party.
March advocates Alaska's secession from the United States, prayer in schools, legalised casino gambling and, says his brochure, "a return to good, old fashion (sic) family values."
The last word on the Nov. 5 election may have been encapsulated on a Washington-area bumper sticker. Its entire message: "Whatever."
